titulo: The signs you can read are the ones that trick you
subtitulo: Italian looks readable, and that is the problem — chiuso, riservato, guasto, and the words that mean something else
cena: You are standing at a door with a printed sign on it, and everyone else in the street has already understood something you have not.
frasePiso: You do not need to read the whole sign. You need to know whether it means go in, come back later, or use another door.

steps.pt: Italian signs look readable, which is the trap. Some words mean exactly what you think. A few do not, and those are the expensive ones.

steps.es: Chiuso per ferie. Riapriamo il ventidue agosto.
steps.pt: Closed for holidays. We reopen on the twenty-second of August.
steps.tts: Chiuso per ferie. Riapriamo il ventidue agosto.
steps.acao: Read the reopening date, not the word. Come back on the twenty-second.

steps.pt: Aperto and chiuso are the whole game. Open and closed, on every door in the country.

steps.es: Orario continuato. Aperto tutti i giorni.
steps.pt: Open through the day. Open every day.
steps.tts: Orario continuato. Aperto tutti i giorni.
steps.acao: Stop planning around a break. This one is open straight through.

steps.pt: Now the false friends. Camera is a room, not a camera. Fattoria is a farm, not a factory. Morbido is soft, not morbid.

steps.promptPt: The sign is long and you only need one thing. Ask whether the place is open. Speak now.
steps.pt: Excuse me, is it open?

steps.es: Riservato ai clienti. Guasto — fuori servizio.
steps.pt: Reserved for customers. Broken — out of service.
steps.tts: Riservato ai clienti. Guasto, fuori servizio.
steps.acao: Buy something or step out, and find the other machine.

steps.pt: Guasto is broken. Fuori servizio is out of order. Both mean the same thing to you: find the other machine.

steps.promptPt: You are looking at a word you do not know. Ask what it means. Speak now.
steps.pt: What does this mean?
Doors: spingere is push, tirare is pull. Entrata in, uscita out. Vietato means forbidden, and it is always serious.

steps.promptPt: The hours are handwritten and unreadable. Ask when they open. Speak now.
steps.pt: What time do you open?

steps.es: Alle sedici. Ora facciamo la pausa.
steps.pt: At four. We're on the break now.
steps.tts: Alle sedici. Ora facciamo la pausa.
steps.acao: Do not wait outside. Come back at four and use the two hours.

steps.pt: Sedici is sixteen — the twenty-four hour clock. Written hours are almost always in it, spoken ones often are too.

steps.promptPt: Ask whether there is an afternoon break, using the frame from B08. Speak now.
steps.pt: Is there an afternoon break?

steps.promptPt: This door says uscita. Ask where the way in is. Speak now.
steps.pt: Where is the entrance?

steps.promptPt: The sign says riservato and you are not sure it applies to you. Ask. Speak now.
steps.pt: May I come in?

steps.promptPt: They read the sign aloud too fast. Ask them to write the time down. Speak now.
steps.pt: Can you write it down for me?

steps.promptPt: Confirm the closed day so you do not walk back for nothing. Speak now.
steps.pt: Are you closed on Mondays?

steps.es: Scusi, è aperto? Cosa vuol dire questo? A che ora aprite?
steps.pinyin: SKOO-zee eh a-PER-to. KO-za vwol DEE-re KWES-to. a keh O-ra a-PREE-te
steps.pt: Shadow the three questions that unlock any door.
steps.tts: Scusi, è aperto? Cosa vuol dire questo? A che ora aprite?

steps.pt: B10 done. Aperto and chiuso, guasto and vietato, spingere and tirare — and cosa vuol dire questo for everything else.

secoes.titulo: The five words that decide the door
secoes.corpo: Aperto, chiuso, entrata, uscita, vietato. Recognise those and you have handled most doors in Italy without reading a single full sentence.

secoes.titulo: False friends that cost money or time
secoes.corpo: Camera is a hotel room. Fattoria is a farm. Morbido is soft. Pretendere is to demand, not to pretend. Attualmente means currently, not actually. None of these are exotic — they are the ones that look safest.

Closed for holidays, most visibly in August, when whole streets of small shops shut for two or three weeks. The sign usually gives the reopening date, so the useful move is reading the date rather than the word.
Many shops outside big-city centres still close in the early afternoon and reopen around four. Orario continuato on the door means the opposite: open straight through.

permissao: You are allowed to ask what a word means while standing in front of the sign that has it. Pointing at a printed word and asking cosa vuol dire questo is a normal thing to do — it is faster than the phone, and it is not an admission that you should have known.
espelho: Anyone who has stood in front of a laundromat sign in their own country trying to work out whether it applies today knows this feeling. Italian makes it worse only because the words look like ones you already own.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You arrive at a small shop at half past two on a weekday and it is dark and shuttered, with no explanation on the door.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: They have gone out of business, or the hours online were wrong.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Outside the big-city centres many small businesses still close for a few hours in the early afternoon and reopen in the late afternoon. A door that says orario continuato is announcing the exception, not the rule.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Read the sign for the reopening hour rather than the word, or ask a che ora aprite? at the bar next door. Then plan the afternoon around four o'clock.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You stop stacking errands into a window that was never open, and you get the same shop with a rested person behind the counter.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not in big-city tourist centres, station areas or supermarkets, where continuous hours are now standard — and increasingly not in Milan, where the pausa has largely disappeared.
